newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn may have to scrap gold plan for '97 - economist.
newsitem.headline: Bonn may have to scrap gold plan for '97 - economist.

text.p: The German government is likely to be forced to abandon its plan to push through a revaluation of the Bundesbank's gold reserves this year, a leading German economist said on Monday.

Horst Siebert, president of the Kiel Institute fuer Weltwirtschaft (IFW), one of Germany's leading economic institutes, told the Handelsblatt newspaper that he agreed with the Bundesbank that forcing through the revaluation would hurt its independence.
This could also hurt the European Central Bank as the Bundesbank was a particular role model for the future European monetary policy-making group.
If Bonn persisted in pushing through the plan to revalue reserves the result would be either a "very big monetary union" or a delay in the planned 1999 launch, he said.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has proposed a revaluation of central bank reserves this year and called for a payout of the book profits this would create in 1997 and 1998.

The Bundesbank opposes the idea of paying out this unrealised profit before the decision has even been reached on which countries qualify for European monetary union, saying this is not in line with European Union guidelines.

Siebert said that, like the Bundesbank, he was not against the idea of revaluing the reserves per se, but was opposed to the timing, fearing this could undermine the interpretation of the economic criteria for entry to monetary union.
"The rules on the valuation ought to be left to the Bundesbank," he said.
